extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics instructors, TAs, and students learning proof-writing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for instructors (and advanced students) on types of mathematical proof and strategies for teaching and writing proofs, including classroom activities, common pitfalls, and examples to use. Covers particular proof forms (contradiction, induction, epsilon-delta, auxiliary functions) and pedagogical techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure proofs with sufficient rigor without excessive detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Students who are new to proofs will need guidance for how to structure proofs and how to be sufficiently rigorous without going into too much detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide individual feedback on assignments; teach students how to balance necessary rigor and concision so proofs are correct but not overburdened with trivial detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point out peculiarities of particular kinds of proof and discuss strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Point out to the class peculiarities of particular kinds of proof and discuss proof-writing strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use class discussions to help students discern when and how to apply various kinds of proof; give targeted examples for each proof type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction — clearly signal and evaluate necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: When using proof by contradiction, clearly signal this (e.g., 'Assume for the sake of contradiction that...') and consider whether contradiction is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use in-class activities that demonstrate that sometimes proofs by contradiction would work better as direct proofs; discuss Gowers' weblog on when contradiction is necessary and Henry Cohn's commentary on dangers of contradiction and ways to avoid them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the dangers of proof by contradiction where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of the potential dangers of proof by contradiction and consider strategies for avoiding those dangers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss Henry Cohn's points about pitfalls of contradiction and suggest alternative direct approaches when they yield clearer or safer arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by induction — use clear examples and expose logical flaws
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach induction using illustrative proofs and counterexamples; expose common logical flaws (e.g., the flawed 'all cows are the same color' proof).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show both correct induction proofs and flawed attempts (assign exercises like identifying the logical flaw) so students learn the structure and limits of induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of auxiliary functions in proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach how to use auxiliary functions as a tool in proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide lesson plans and examples demonstrating how constructing an auxiliary function can facilitate a proof; give concrete worked examples students can emulate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epsilon-delta and similar analytic proofs: choose constants then present concise proof
rubrics_metrics.description: In epsilon-delta proofs, it is conventional to choose a constant so that a specific property holds without fully justifying the specific choice in the final concise proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Help students by first giving an example that shows how to choose the constant (work the choice out in detail), then demonstrate how to write the conventionally concise proof that follows from that choice (example: proving existence of x with x^2 = 2 as in Bartle & Sherbert).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit revisions and avoid rewarding speed/cleverness
rubrics_metrics.description: Design courses to avoid common pitfalls like rewarding speed and 'ostentatious displays of cleverness' and instead allow resubmission and revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cathy O'Neil's proof-writing course permits unlimited revisions to encourage careful reasoning over quick, showy solutions; adopt policies that value clarity and correctness over speed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof-scrambling activities to teach logical order and connectors
rubrics_metrics.description: Use proof-scrambling activities where students must correctly order scrambled sentences of a proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These activities help students identify when a proof is logically correct, recognize how authors use words like 'therefore' and 'next' to indicate direction of logic, and gain experience reading and comprehending proofs (from Russell E. Goodman).

rubrics_metrics.name: Signal logical flow with connective words and explicit structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach students to use words and phrases that indicate the direction of logic and structure of a proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight usage of transition words ('therefore', 'next', 'assume', etc.) and show example proofs with guiding text (e.g., Peter Shor's proof with guiding text) so students learn to guide the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use accessible subject matter to introduce logic and motivate proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce logical principles using accessible subject matter (puzzle problems, simple examples) to motivate the need for proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Susanna Epp recommends using accessible content to help undergraduates construct simple proofs and disproofs and to motivate why rigorous proof is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide examples of elegant proofs and curated resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Show students examples of elegant proofs and point them to textbooks and collections of elegant proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use resources such as Proofs from THE BOOK, Charming Proofs, HOW TO THINK LIKE A MATHEMATICIAN, and other listed texts; present model 'elegant' proofs (e.g., the pigeonhole principle example) to illustrate style and economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use focused recitations addressing strategies, structure, and elegance
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate recitations or focused sessions on proof-writing strategies, proof structure, and proof elegance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The MIT Real Analysis recitations (Strategies for proof writing; Proof-writing strategies and proof structure; Proof elegance) serve as examples to structure sessions that teach these aspects explicitly.
